title: Stochastic trace sampler and stage synthesis
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a lightweight, reproducible protocol for collecting representative e2e traces with an emphasis on tail behavior (p95–p99+) while controlling for cache state, batching pressure, and sequence-length mix. Goal is to produce stage-attributed trace sets that are small enough to iterate on but rich enough to reproduce rare pathologies.

Key ideas / motivation:
- The usual uniform sampling over requests misses correlated microbursts and coldstart cascades. We need a stochastic sampler that intentionally oversamples low-representation regimes (cold KV-miss, long-seqlen, cross-model fallbacks).
- Weight traces by a small vector of features (seqlen bucket, cache-hit boolean, routing-tier, client-qps bucket) and schedule pulls with a phase-reservoir so we see both steady-state and bursty episodes.
- Store stage-level timing (tokenize, encode, kv-lookup, batch-wait, kernel-exec, emit, egress) with event ids so we can stitch and replay.

Sampler design (phase-reservoir approach):
1) Feature buckets to compute sampling weight (produced from light telemetry):
   - seqlen: 0-32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+
   - cache_state: hot / warm / cold (hot=prefix hit, warm=partial KV hit)
   - client_tier: hosted | dedicated | private
   - qps_bucket: <1, 1-5, 6-20, 21+
2) Base weight = 1 / sqrt(bucket_frequency) (approx inversely proportional to rarity).
3) Phase-reservoir: maintain a short-term reservoir per weight-class to ensure microburst contexts are preserved. Reservoir retention = 10s of requests per reservoir. Every N seconds pick one from each non-empty reservoir for export.
4) Stochastic jitter envelope: random offset on the pick time (0–200ms) to avoid aligning with a single upstream scheduler.

Trace capture fields (must be included in exported JSON traces):
- trace_id, timestamp, client_id, route, model_version, seq_len, prompt_tokens, response_tokens, stage_timings: list of (stage_name, start_ns, end_ns), cache_hint, batch_id, cpu_ms, gpu_ms, host, region, notes
- include a small snapshot of batch composition (token counts per request in batch) where batch_wait occurred.

Cohorts to capture (for experiments):
- Coldstart cohort: requests with cache_state=cold and model_warm=false within 60s window after model load.
- Hot long-seqlen: cache_state=hot & seq_len>=512. Purpose: observe KV eviction pressure + kernel-exec scaling.
- Fallback cascade: route where initial model > fallback model occurred. Look for cascading latency increase at emit/egress stage.
- Microburst cohort: qps_bucket=21+ and batch_size variance >2 within 500ms window.

Stage taxonomy (how we break down the e2e path):
- tokenization (preprocessing)
- request-serialize (ingress)
- routing-decision (smart-routing + policy checks)
- batch-wait (time waiting for batch formation)
- kv-lookup (prefix KV cache access + memlocal fallback)
- model-exec (kernel launch, attention compute, kv-restore)
- emit-stage (postprocess, safety checks, tool-calls)
- egress (network serialize + TLS + client ack)

Hypotheses we want to test quickly:
H1: p99 in hot long-seqlen cohort is dominated by model-exec variance, not batch-wait. If true => focus on kernel scheduling and preemption windows.
H2: coldstart cohort p95 shifts toward kv-lookup + batch-wait; small targeted warming (micro-prefetch) reduces tail by >20%.
H3: microburst cohort shows correlated batch-wait spikes across multiple hosts due to synchronized scheduler heartbeat; adding random jitter to scheduler wake reduces p99 across hosts.

Quick experiments (short checklist):
- [ ] Deploy sampler stable branch (PR 4823) to prod-capture with sample rate=1/500 for 24h (make sure to tag captured traces). Command: tools/trace-capture --config sampler-phase-reservoir.yaml --out s3://redwood-traces/stochastic/2024-09-24
- [ ] Run synthetic generator to create 1k coldstart traces (script: infra/synthetic_load/coldstart_burst.py --duration 120 --seqlen 128)
- [ ] Run replay harness to measure stage-level p50/p95/p99 and emit CSV per-cohort: tools/trace-replay --input s3://... --cohort coldstart --output ./results/coldstart.csv
- [ ] Spotlight: compare kernel_exec tail across GPU types (A100 vs H100) for model v3 and quantized-v3. (linked_pr: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4898)

Preliminary findings (from 2024-09-20 dev capture):
- Hot seqlen 512+ p99 dominated by spikes in model-exec (long tail correlated with off-chip memory stalls in 2 hosts). Evidence: host-level gpu-ms distribution shows heavy right tail on two hosts; batch_wait median near zero during those traces.
- Coldstart p95 was a mix: kv-lookup retries on memcached layer + batch-wait. There were several traces with kv-lookup >120ms where underlying eviction logs (host 12) matched.
- Microburst sampling revealed that our previous fixed-schedule sampler missed 40% of burst episodes; the phase-reservoir recovered these.

Open questions / TO-DOs:
- What is the safe retention period for reservoirs before privacy/PII concerns? (ask security/legal)
- Should the sampler include model-input hashes for exact deduping? Hashing strategy needs review (avoid leaking prompt PII).
- Determine export size ceiling per day for S3 storage (ops help needed). Current estimate: 200MB/day at 1/500 sample rate.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally experimental: the sampler will be toggled on/off via safe flags and only export anonymized traces.
- Look at PR 4823 for Golang implementation details; sampling weights are defined in sampler/weights.go.
- If you want to reproduce the preliminary numbers, pull trace bundle: s3://redwood-traces/dev/stochastic/2024-09-20/bundle.tgz (access group: eng-serving-runtime-only)

Next steps (short horizon):
- Finalize privacy checklist with Security by EOD 2024-10-06.
- Run 72-hour capture at 1/1000 with reservoir size tune to 20s; analyze p99 deltas per-cohort.
- If coldstart warming hypothesis holds, prototype micro-prefetch and measure cost vs tail reduction.

Appendix: quick heuristics for analysis scripts
- Top-stage decomposition CSV: columns = trace_id, cohort, stage, duration_ms, host, model, seqlen
- Quick awk command to get p99 of model-exec: awk -F"," '\\$3=="model-exec" {print \\\$(4)}' traces.csv | python -c 'import sys, numpy as np; print(np.percentile(list(map(float, sys.stdin)),99))'
